subsection: 6. The US economy, 1945–1968: sources of the boom and the multinational corporation

notes.h: The wartime base of the boom
notes.b: The Great Depression of the 1930s left the United States with high unemployment, and it was the Second World War that finally ended it. The war then left the country with an industrial economy far stronger than any rival's, and that was the platform for the postwar boom.
points: The United States entered the war after the attack on Pearl Harbor on 7 December 1941. Between 1941 and 1945 its factories turned out vast numbers of aircraft, ships, tanks and munitions, so jobs were plentiful.
Unemployment fell to very low levels, about 1 to 2 per cent at its lowest, in 1944, which ended the Depression.

The United States was never bombed or invaded, so its factories survived intact. In 1945 it produced about half of the world's manufactured goods, while its European and Japanese rivals had been devastated by the war.

Rationing, wage and price controls and war bonds meant households could not spend freely during the war, so they saved heavily. When rationing and controls ended in 1945-46 families had large sums to spend.

Wartime shortages of consumer goods also built up a pent-up demand (buying that had been held back and was now released) for cars, houses and household appliances after 1945, which kept factories busy once war orders fell.

The Servicemen's Readjustment Act, known as the GI Bill and signed in June 1944, paid tuition and living allowances for veterans, offered government-guaranteed loans for homes, farms and businesses, and gave unemployment allowances for a year.

The GI Bill's home loans helped to create a mass market for housing, which fed demand for consumer goods and for the construction industry. In practice black veterans often met discrimination in access to loans and colleges, especially in the South.

The wartime government became the largest customer in the economy and built many plants itself, in industries such as aluminium, synthetic rubber and aircraft. The Surplus Property Act of 1944 arranged their sale after 1945, and large firms bought most of them cheaply.
notes.tip: For the 'why did the economy boom' essay, give a stated list of causes and link or rank them rather than listing them, using dated examples such as the GI Bill (1944). Always add the caveat that black veterans were often denied GI Bill benefits in practice.

notes.h: International financing: Bretton Woods and Marshall Aid
notes.b: The United States also designed the postwar international money system and paid for much of Western Europe's recovery. Both made the dollar the central currency and gave American firms customers abroad. This setting was the Cold War, in which the US aimed to contain Soviet influence and wanted strong trading partners.
points: The Bretton Woods conference of July 1944 in New Hampshire created the International Monetary Fund (IMF), which supports exchange rates with short-term loans, and the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (the World Bank), which lends for reconstruction and development.

Under the Bretton Woods system the US dollar was convertible to gold at 35 dollars an ounce and other currencies were pegged (fixed) to the dollar. This made the dollar the reserve currency, the one other countries held to settle international trade.

War-damaged Europe could not earn enough dollars to buy what it needed, a shortage known as the dollar gap. American loans and aid filled it, and they were spent on US goods, so the dollar's role helped US exporters. It also let American companies invest abroad cheaply.

The Marshall Plan (European Recovery Program) of 1948 to 1952 gave about 13 billion dollars to Western European states, after George Marshall announced it in June 1947. Much of it was spent on American goods, which boosted US exports and revived trading partners.

The Korean War began in June 1950, and NSC-68 (a policy paper of April 1950) urged a large rearmament. Defence spending roughly quadrupled between 1950 and 1953, so rearmament added a great deal of demand to the economy.

The General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT), signed in 1947 and in force from 1948, committed the United States and other states to lower trade barriers (limits such as tariffs on imports). This suited the world's biggest exporter.
notes.tip: Do not confuse the Marshall Plan (1948-52, aid), the Truman Doctrine (1947, Greece and Turkey) and Bretton Woods (1944, the monetary system). Also keep the IMF (exchange rates, short-term loans) separate from the World Bank (reconstruction and development loans).

notes.h: Public investment: highways, defence and research
notes.b: The federal government did not leave growth to the market alone. Spending on roads, defence, science and education built up whole industries in the 1950s and 1960s.
points: The Federal-Aid Highway Act of 1956, signed by Eisenhower, funded an Interstate Highway System of about 41,000 miles. It opened up suburban development and boosted car production and steel.

The Interstate programme was paid for from a Highway Trust Fund financed by fuel taxes. It was also justified on defence grounds, such as evacuating cities and moving troops, and Eisenhower had been impressed by the German autobahns.
Federal defence spending stayed high through the 1950s and 1960s, which supplied a large and steady market for aircraft, electronics and missile manufacturers.

Defence research paid for the development of jet aircraft, radar, nuclear power for submarines and later computers. These spin-offs (civilian uses of military technology) then spread into civilian industry.
The National Science Foundation was created in 1950, and federal research funding grew steadily, with universities acting as partners to government research.
The Soviet Union launched Sputnik in October 1957, and the United States founded NASA in 1958. The space programme then employed thousands of engineers and contractors in the 1960s.
The National Defense Education Act of 1958 funded science, mathematics and foreign-language teaching and student loans, because Sputnik made Americans fear they were falling behind in science.
notes.tip: Examiners ask why the Interstate system was built and why defence spending grew, so give the economic reason (cars, steel, suburbs) and the defence reason together. Do not mix up the NSF (1950) and NASA (1958), or the GI Bill (1944), the Highway Act (1956) and the National Defense Education Act (1958).

notes.b: Large, lasting defence budgets created a network of armed forces, contractors and politicians with a shared interest in keeping spending high. The military-industrial complex is the name given to that alliance, and Eisenhower warned of it as he left office.
points: Eisenhower's farewell address was broadcast on 17 January 1961, three days before he left office. He said: "we must guard against the acquisition of unwarranted influence, whether sought or unsought, by the military-industrial complex."

He also noted a "conjunction of an immense military establishment and a large arms industry" that was new in American experience. His point was about influence over policy, not an attack on defence spending in general.

Major defence contractors such as Lockheed, Boeing, General Dynamics and Douglas received large government contracts, and many companies depended on them for much of their revenue, so they had a strong interest in high defence budgets.
The warning came from a former general whose own administration had built up the nuclear arsenal and relied on it. Critics raised this irony to argue that he had helped create the problem.

Defence and space contracts fuelled growth in California and later Silicon Valley (the electronics and semiconductor centre). A stable source of contracts encouraged high-technology industries, including computing.

Critics argued that the complex distorted national priorities, because money and skilled scientists were drawn to weapons rather than to schools, housing or civilian needs. C. Wright Mills's The Power Elite was an earlier critical study of a small group of leaders.
notes.tip: For this topic, say who said it, when (17 January 1961), what it meant and which companies were involved, then judge whether the warning was justified. Naming the date earns credit, and do not claim Eisenhower criticised defence spending in general.

notes.h: Key personality: the Organization Man (William H. Whyte's type of corporate employee)
notes.b: The Organization Man is not a single real person but a type: a salaried corporate manager or professional who moved with the company. William H. Whyte named the type in 1956. It shows corporate capitalism, an economy dominated by large corporations run by salaried managers.
points: William H. Whyte, an editor at Fortune magazine, published The Organization Man in 1956 as a study of white-collar workers (office and managerial employees) in large corporations and suburban communities.
Whyte argued that the corporate employee had accepted a social ethic that valued belonging, teamwork and conformity over individualism and personal conscience.
The social ethic had three beliefs: that the group is the source of creativity, that belonging is the individual's greatest need, and that science can be applied to achieve belonging.

Whyte studied Park Forest, Illinois, a planned suburb outside Chicago of young corporate families who moved often and valued being sociable. He also criticised the personality tests companies used in hiring, which rewarded fitting in.

The Organization Man was a salaried manager or professional, often moving between cities and suburbs as the company required. His career depended on loyalty to the corporation and on fitting in with its expectations.

Other writers shared the worry about conformity. David Riesman's The Lonely Crowd (1950) described the other-directed person, guided by the approval of others, and C. Wright Mills's White Collar (1951) described anxious salaried workers.
Sloan Wilson's novel The Man in the Gray Flannel Suit (1955) portrayed a similar figure, an executive torn between career success and family life.
Contemporaries praised the corporation for stability, security and rising living standards, but many critics saw the Organization Man as a threat to individual creativity and independence.
Historians use the figure as a useful portrait of 1950s corporate culture and conformity, though later scholars argue that the book overstated the conformity of American corporate life.
notes.tip: Describe the Organization Man as a type, not a person, and give Whyte, the book and 1956, the social ethic with its three beliefs, and Park Forest. Keep Whyte (1956), Riesman (1950), Wilson (1955) and Mills (1951) apart.

notes.b: A multinational corporation is a company that owns and runs operations in several countries. From the 1950s American multinationals expanded overseas, which is a key part of globalisation, the growing integration of national economies through trade, investment and multinationals.
points: General Motors, IBM, Coca-Cola and the International Telephone and Telegraph Corporation (ITT) were large US multinationals with big overseas operations by the 1960s. They spread by direct investment, subsidiaries, franchises and local bottlers, and the purchase of existing firms.

IBM's World Trade Corporation, created in 1949 to run IBM's overseas business, shows how a company could organise itself for the world market. By the 1960s a large share of IBM's revenue came from outside the United States.
Coca-Cola grew abroad through franchised local bottlers, who bought the syrup and sold the drink in their own market. The system was built up from the 1920s and extended widely after 1945.
General Motors owned Opel in Germany (since 1929) and Vauxhall in Britain (since 1925), and Ford also had European subsidiaries, so American carmakers built and sold cars across Europe.

ITT under Harold Geneen, chief executive from 1959, became a conglomerate (a company owning unrelated businesses) by buying firms in many industries and countries in the 1960s. It later became notorious for its involvement in Chile.

US firms invested heavily in Western Europe after the Treaty of Rome of 1957 created the European Economic Community (in force 1958), a large single market behind a common external tariff. Building plants inside it let them avoid the tariff.
US foreign policy supported the expansion by encouraging open trade and investment, and the strong dollar made it cheap for American companies to buy assets abroad.

Critics in Europe, such as Jean-Jacques Servan-Schreiber in The American Challenge (1967), warned that US firms were taking over key European industries. The Fortune 500 list of the largest American industrial companies, first published in 1955, showed how far a few big firms dominated the economy.
notes.tip: Name General Motors, IBM, Coca-Cola and ITT with a distinct fact for each (IBM's World Trade Corporation in 1949, Coca-Cola franchising, GM in Europe, ITT as a conglomerate). Explain why Western Europe and the Treaty of Rome mattered and give the European criticism. Do not confuse the Treaty of Rome (1957) with the Treaty of Detroit (1950).

notes.h: Organised labour and the postwar bargain
notes.b: The boom was shared with many industrial workers because trade unions were strong in its core industries. Their agreements with large firms tied pay to the growth the corporations enjoyed.
points: Union members reached about a third of non-farm workers in the mid-1950s, concentrated in steel, car manufacturing, mining and transport.

The United Auto Workers and General Motors signed a five-year contract in 1950, often called the Treaty of Detroit. It linked wages to productivity and the cost of living and provided pensions and health insurance, while management kept control of production decisions.
Such agreements gave many manual workers rising real wages and benefits, which means pay that bought more over time, and they became a model for other unions in the core industries.

The Taft-Hartley Act of 1947 restricted union tactics such as secondary boycotts (action against a firm's customers or suppliers) and the closed shop (only hiring union members), and it allowed states to pass right-to-work laws. It also required union leaders to sign non-communist affidavits.
The American Federation of Labor and the Congress of Industrial Organizations merged in 1955 under George Meany, which created a single labour federation.
Unions were weakest in the South and among service and farm workers, who were often excluded from the postwar bargain.
notes.tip: Do not confuse the Treaty of Detroit (1950, a union contract) with the Treaty of Rome (1957). On Taft-Hartley, say only that it required non-communist affidavits from union leaders.

notes.h: Keynesian economic policy: the 1964 tax cut
notes.b: Government economists believed that spending and tax policy could keep growth going, and the 1964 tax cut was the major test of that belief. The idea comes from John Maynard Keynes, who argued that governments can manage demand (the total spending in the economy) through spending and taxation.
points: The economic advisers of Kennedy and Johnson accepted Keynes's ideas. In practice this meant cutting taxes or raising spending to boost demand when growth slowed.

Walter Heller, chairman of the Council of Economic Advisers under Kennedy, argued for a tax cut to stimulate demand and growth, because lower taxes leave households and firms with more to spend and invest.
The Revenue Act of 1964, signed by Johnson, cut taxes and reduced the top income tax rate from 91 per cent to 70 per cent.
Strong economic growth followed in the mid-1960s, so the tax cut is often cited as a successful example of demand management before the costs of the Vietnam War appeared.
Milton Friedman, a monetarist (someone who stresses controlling the money supply), argued that governments could not fine-tune the economy.
notes.tip: Use the 1964 tax cut as a named example of Keynesian demand management, with Heller, Johnson and the cut from 91 to 70 per cent. Mention Friedman only as the critic of fine-tuning.

notes.h: Assessment: achievements and limits of the boom
notes.b: A strong judgement weighs the scale of the boom against its dependence on temporary US dominance and on government spending. It also compares what contemporaries praised with what later critics noticed.
points: Achievement: between 1945 and 1968 living standards rose steadily, home ownership became widespread and a large middle class emerged, helped by the GI Bill and rising union wages.
Limit: the boom depended partly on the temporary dominance of the US economy after 1945, which was bound to decline as Europe and Japan recovered from the war.
Limit: critics argue the boom rested on defence spending and large public investment, such as the Interstate system and research funding, and not only on the free market.

Limit: some groups did not share fully in the boom. Black Americans and many southern workers faced discrimination in jobs and housing, and black veterans were often denied GI Bill benefits in practice.

John Kenneth Galbraith's The Affluent Society (1958) argued that the boom created private wealth but left public services such as schools and parks neglected, an idea summed up as private affluence and public squalor.
Michael Harrington's The Other America (1962) showed that tens of millions still lived in poverty despite the boom.

Contemporary against later views: many at the time praised corporate America for stability and rising living standards, while Whyte's critique of the Organization Man saw conformity and a loss of individualism.
notes.tip: Weigh the causes and show the limits: dependence on defence spending and temporary dominance, plus unequal sharing. Naming Galbraith or Harrington adds weight, as does recognising that the boom was not shared equally.

keyTerms.definition: An economic system dominated by large corporations, with managers and salaried employees, which expanded rapidly in the United States after 1945.
The growing integration of national economies through trade, investment and the activities of multinational companies, which accelerated after 1945.
The network of defence contractors, military officers and politicians whose shared interests promoted high defence spending, a phrase used by Eisenhower in 1961.
A company that owns or controls production in several countries, such as General Motors, IBM and Coca-Cola in this period.
The postwar monetary order agreed in 1944, which made the dollar the central currency and tied other currencies to it, with the dollar convertible to gold.
The Servicemen's Readjustment Act of 1944, which gave veterans education and training benefits, home and business loans and unemployment pay.
The type of corporate employee described by William H. Whyte in his 1956 book, who accepted corporate loyalty and conformity as a way of life.
The network of federally funded motorways authorised by the Federal-Aid Highway Act of 1956, which reshaped American cities, suburbs and the car industry.
The 1950 five-year agreement between General Motors and the United Auto Workers that exchanged union acceptance of management control for rising wages, pensions and health insurance.
